title: Command of Evidence, Part 2: A Hard Question and Common Traps

beats.say: In part one, we learned to find the exact claim, and to turn it into a prediction before reading the choices.
Then we crossed out answers that are inaccurate, and answers that are accurate but irrelevant to the claim.
In this video, we use the method on a hard question about a character, and then look at the traps.
beats.item: Today: a hard question and traps

beats.say: Hard question. Some questions ask which quotation best illustrates a claim about a character. The claim may name two traits, and the quotation must show both.
Tick off each trait in the claim, one by one, and then check each quotation against the list.

scenes.title: Read the text
scenes.text: The narrator of a story portrays Mr. Okafor as generous but proud. He gives away most of his harvest each year, yet he refuses to let anyone repay or even thank him.

beats.say: The claim names two traits, generous, and proud. A good quotation must show both of them.
Our prediction is, we should see him giving something away, and also refusing thanks or help in a proud way.

scenes.title: Which quotation illustrates the claim?
scenes.question: Which quotation from the story best illustrates the claim about Mr. Okafor?

options.A: He rose early each morning to walk the long rows of his field.
options.B: He filled every neighbor's basket, then waved away their thanks without a word.
options.C: He kept his old coat buttoned up against the cold wind.
options.D: He gave a basket to a neighbor, who thanked him warmly.

beats.say: Choice A is a vivid line about his morning routine. It shows neither trait, so it's off-claim.
Choice C is about his coat and the wind. It describes the setting, and doesn't show either trait.
Choice D shows him giving a basket, which is generous. But he accepts thanks, so it misses the proud part.
Choice B shows both. He fills every basket, which is generous, and he waves away thanks, which is proud. The answer is B.
Now the traps. Each one is a way that a careful reader can still pick a wrong answer. We'll see the trap, and then the habit that avoids it.
Trap one. Most wrong choices on a table question are accurate. A true number can still be the wrong answer if it doesn't connect to the claim.
beats.wrong: true number, so it is correct

beats.say: Check relevance as well as accuracy. Ask whether the choice speaks to the exact comparison in the claim.
beats.right: accurate and tied to the claim

beats.say: Trap two. A claim with two parts needs evidence for both parts. Evidence for only one part feels right, but it's incomplete.
Split the claim into its parts, and make sure the choice answers each one.
Trap three. A hypothesis is about a certain group. A finding about a different group doesn't test it, even if it sounds related.
Match the group in the evidence to the group in the claim. If they differ, move on.
Trap four. Students read the stem too fast and answer backward. A question that asks to weaken the claim wants the opposite of support.
beats.wrong: pick evidence that fits the claim

beats.say: Underline the verb in the question, support or weaken, before you do anything else.
Trap five. A beautifully written line about the setting can look like good evidence. But a line must illustrate the trait in the claim.
beats.wrong: a lovely line about the weather

beats.say: Choose the plain line that shows the trait, even if it's less pretty.
beats.right: a plain line showing both traits

beats.say: To recap. Accurate isn't enough. The choice must be relevant, must cover every part of the claim, and must be about the right group.
Read the verb in the question, support or weaken, and choose quotations that show every trait.
beats.item: Check the verb; check every trait

beats.say: In the next topic, we study inferences, where you complete a logical conclusion from the text.
